text:
Science & Tech Daily Brief | September 17, 2026

Eight research and technology developments from September 16 worth watching.

1. Multiple materials on one photonics platform

Researchers transferred single-crystal nanomembranes onto silicon and silicon-nitride photonic circuits.

The devices included a barium titanate modulator above 23 GHz, cobalt ferrite optical components, and GaAs and GaN photodetectors.

The idea could combine functions that one material cannot provide. Wafer-scale manufacturing remains the next test.

2. SK hynix explores U.S. memory production

Reuters reported early talks between SK hynix and Intel over possible U.S. memory production.

Options include using Intel’s Ohio facilities or forming a broader venture.

Nothing has been agreed. A deal could extend U.S. AI supply-chain localization from packaging into memory fabrication.

3. Paper2Agent turns papers into AI agents

Paper2Agent reads papers, data and code, then generates MCP tools that expose research methods through natural language.

The team converted 74 of 100 computational biology papers into agents, with 593 of 599 generated tools passing automated validation.

The benchmark was developer-built, and accessible code and data remain important constraints.

4. A reusable DNA computer calculates through chemistry

Researchers built DNA circuits that compute by relaxing toward thermodynamic equilibrium.

The system ran ten programs, reached 100-bit calculations and reused some circuits up to 25 times.

Larger calculations slowed sharply, so this remains an experimental molecular computer.

5. Human brain organoids integrated into mouse neural circuits

Researchers transplanted human cortical organoids into mice missing large parts of their normal cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons.

The human tissue integrated with the mouse nervous system and showed organized activity and measurable behavioral effects.

It offers a new research platform, not a human brain or human-level cognition.

6. Thorium-229 detected with continuous-wave laser light

Researchers excited thorium-229 nuclei in calcium fluoride using a continuous-wave laser near 148 nm and detected the transition through absorption.

That could simplify solid-state nuclear spectroscopy and future nuclear clocks.

It is not yet a working clock, and stability and accuracy remain unresolved.

7. A superconductor showed electrically controllable memory

Direct-current pulses switched UTe₂ between metastable superconducting states with different critical currents.

The material retained its previous state and could later be reset.

The effect still requires unusual crystals, very low temperatures and strong magnetic fields.

8. A simulation links early black holes with JWST’s little red dots

A cosmological simulation grew a roughly one-million-solar-mass black-hole seed to around 30 million solar masses through super-Eddington accretion.

Its surrounding material also produced features resembling JWST’s little red dots.

It is a possible explanation, not an observation of black-hole formation itself.

Today’s line

Today’s research pushed computation and information into photonic chips, DNA, brain tissue, atomic nuclei and superconductors.

The next test is scale.

The Fed just hiked 25 bps to 3.75%–4.00%, its first-rate hike since 2023.

Markets closed mixed (Dow down 90 pts, Nasdaq +0.5%) because futures had already priced 92% of the move. But looking under the hood of today's SEP release and Chair Warsh's presser, the macro tape just underwent a quiet regime change:

The Unanimous Shift:

▪ 12–0 vote. July's three hawkish dissenters carried the entire committee without a single dissent. 
▪ Median dots revised up to 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027 (up from 3.8% and 3.6% in June). 
▪ 12 of 18 officials pencil in another hike before year-end; 4 sit higher. 
▪ 17 of 18 participants see inflation risks weighted strictly to the upside.

The Inflation & Curve Dynamic:

▪ Headline CPI sticky at 3.4% forced the Fed's hand. Warsh confirmed they had to "remove a dose of accommodation" with inflation too high for too long. 
▪ The front end now migrates toward 4% to meet a long end that moved months ago (10Y 4.95%, 30Y at 5.31%).

The Portfolio Implication:

Earning 4% in cash feels safe during a mixed session, but it masks compounding reinvestment risk as the curve shifts.

The easing cycle isn't paused; it’s reversed. Institutional balance sheets require deliberate duration laddering and non-correlated assets that do not price off Fed accommodation.

text:
THE SCHOOL OF LIFE: By Kevin Holten
    Did you like going to school when you were a kid?  Maybe you did.  But you still loved high school graduation day and the freedom it offered.  And yet, you also wondered about what you were going to do next.  And maybe you even feared the future a little.
    Well, those days are long gone.  But guess what.  You’re still a student.  A student of life.  And every day is a classroom from which you need to graduate.  That’s just the way it is.
    Do you find that perspective to be a little depressing?  Maybe you do.  But remember this: it’s the same for all eight billion of us currently living on this planet, as it was for all those who came before us.  And graduation day is coming and it’ll be the greatest and most glorious day of your life.
    So, chin up.  Because “you ain’t seen nothing yet”.  The best is yet to come.
    Meanwhile, so many of us dream of the day when we will finally be happy: when we are out of debt, driving the car we always wanted, living in the house we always dreamed of, and doing what we love to do.
    But here’s lesson number one in the school of life that might take you, like me, a lifetime to learn: fantasizing about future happiness doesn’t bring fulfillment.  Living fully in the moment does.
    We fight that every day, don’t we?  And why?  Because we so often choose to focus on the negatives when a mountain of positives is sitting right there in front of us.  At least I do.  And then I must slap myself, again.
    Still, no matter what you choose to do, graduation day is coming and it’ll be the greatest and most glorious day of your life.
    So, let’s do a little experiment.  Go find yourself a tree, lean against it and watch the sunset.  Be sure to bring a pen and a notepad with you.  Why?  Because you need to make a list of all the memories that come to your mind as you sit there. 
    And if I’m correct, your list is not going to be about a bunch of Super Bowls.  It’s going to be a lot of little things.  Little things that meant little back then but mean so much now.
    What are my little things?  Sitting on grandma’s couch while she teaches me how to tie my shoelaces.  My mother comforting me in my room at night when I can’t get to sleep.  Or like I did, coming up with stories at bedtime to put my son to sleep and him laughing so hard he couldn’t get to sleep.
    And there are other things like playing in the ocean of grain in the grain truck during harvest.  Laughing uncontrollably at something my uncle said at dinner on Christmas Eve.  Seeing how my dad looked at us as my little boy and I boarded an airplane.
    Silly things, right?  Not silly at all.  Cherished memories.  You get them every day like snowflakes floating from the sky.  Take the time to notice them.  And if you do, you’ll realize how rich you are.
    Legendary UCLA basketball coach John Wooden said that little things make big things happen.  That’s why they are so important.
    Such a simple thing to learn.  And that’s your lesson for today.  Now, go outside and play.

SOURCE: KEVIN HOLTEN BISMARCK TRIBUNE

"Blow to Russia’s Defense Industry: Uzbekistan Swaps Su-30s for Chinese J-10s [title]

Uzbekistan has switched its fighter jet supplier, opting for Chinese aircraft over Russian ones. An expert has revealed the decisive factor behind this move.

Uzbekistan has passed over Russian Su-30SM fighter jets in favor of the Chinese J-10CE. Six of the aircraft have already been delivered to the country's Air Force. Writing for *https://t.co/eJYzJSW9rw*, analyst Ruslan Ramazanov attributed the choice to financial reasons: the cost of the Chinese aircraft proved to be significantly lower than the Russian alternative. The decision followed a comparison of price offers from both countries, with cost emerging as the deciding factor.

The export price of the J-10CE is estimated at approximately $40–50 million per unit, whereas the Russian heavy Su-30 fighter costs foreign buyers $50–60 million. A $10 million difference per aircraft translates to potential savings of around $60 million when purchasing six jets. The exact value of the Uzbek contract has not been officially disclosed; the figures cited are based on *https://t.co/eJYzJSW9rw* estimates rather than official documents from the parties involved.

China also offered logistics support packages for aircraft maintenance. According to Ramazanov, these packages could reduce the fighter's total lifecycle costs by 30–40%. The benefits of choosing the Chinese aircraft extend beyond the initial purchase price; operating the J-10CE promises to be cheaper in the long run as well. For the customer, this means the economic benefit spans the entire service life of the fleet, rather than being limited to the time of the transaction." Voenni Strannitzi-Rus, 16Sept

text:
Isaiah Likely | TE | NYG: 2026 projection

Isaiah Likely enters his fifth year in the league with a fresh start on a new team, and the early returns point to an entirely different ceiling than what fantasy managers saw during his time in Baltimore. Last season, playing in 12 games, he managed 5.14 fantasy points per game on a 55.9 percent snap share and a 12 percent target share. The volume was thin, hovering around 3.0 opportunities per game, though he did salvage some utility with 0.5 red zone opportunities per game. Entering this season, the situation shifted dramatically. He joins a New York offense operating at 63.5 plays per game with a market implied team total of 22.3 points, though the scheme leans slightly toward the run with a -4.7 pass rate over expected. Crucially, the vacated work in his new environment is massive, featuring 25.5 percent of the position room work now vacant and 51.6 percent of team targets now vacant. That departure of previous production opened the door for an immediate featured role as the clear tight end one on the depth chart. The opening week performance blew past all historical baselines. In that initial outing against Dallas, he commanded 8 targets, turning all 8 receptions into a massive 27.8 fantasy point explosion. That single game vastly outperformed his preseason projection of 5.93 points, shifting the model firmly into bullish territory despite a modest projection baseline of 3.17 targets per game across the full slate. The glaring risk with Likely centers on sustainability. Tight end scoring relies heavily on efficiency when raw target volume is low, and a single game spike of 27.8 points naturally introduces regression risk if the weekly target share settles back toward his historical norms. The offense is not an elite passing juggernaut, and the negative pass rate over expected means he will need to maintain high efficiency on limited team pass volume to pay off the new starting price. Yet, the sheer size of the vacated team targets and his locked-in starting role give him a stable foundation that his previous backup days never offered. Fantasy managers must weigh the explosive week one ceiling against the reality of a run-leaning offense and a thin historical target baseline.

What to watch:
• Monitor whether the eight-target volume from week one holds steady or regresses toward his historical three-target baseline.
• Watch how the offense balances its run-leaning pass rate over expected against his newly established role as the clear top tight end.
• Track his red zone usage to see if he converts the high vacated target share into high-value scoring opportunities.
• Observe if the heavy weight of the preseason projection continues to drag down his rest-of-season model outlook despite the massive week one output.

text:
DEARBORN, Michigan (WWJ) -- Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud has offered Macklemore a free, city-sponsored concert in Metro Detroit, a day after the rapper was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour over pro-Palestinian remarks he made onstage.

“If they don’t want you performing in their stadiums, you’re always welcome in Dearborn,” Hammoud posted on social media on Monday night. “Come put on a show here. We’ll make it a free concert, sponsored by the City, and help make it one of the best around. We stand with you and for a free Palestine. Let’s make it happen.”

It’s not clear whether Macklemore will accept. He had not publicly responded to the invitation as of Tuesday.
Dearborn has the largest Muslim population per capita in the United States, and Hammoud, elected in 2021, was the city’s first Arab American and first Muslim mayor.

In a statement Tuesday evening, ADL Michigan regional director Elyssa Schmier called Hammoud’s offering to Macklemore was “deeply concerning.”

“No mayor should put up public funds for a concert with someone who has a well-documented history of antisemitic rhetoric,” Schmier said. “Elected officials have a responsibility to represent all constituents. At a time of heightened tensions and rising antisemitism nationally and in Michigan, Mayor Hammoud’s invitation, and the city funding attached to it, risks further alienating Jewish residents rather than building the trust his office should be modeling.”

Macklemore released his debut album in 2005. This month, Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour, and he described the two as friends. During at least two performances, Macklemore spoke about his support for Palestinians. Macklemore posted a recording of his remarks on Sept. 7 on his social media with the caption, “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.”

“One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he told the crowd.

The remarks drew national attention and criticism. The Anti-Defamation League called Macklemore’s comments unacceptable, and the Israeli American Council circulated a petition seeking his removal from the rest of the tour.

Macklemore’s removal from the tour became public Monday. As CBS News reported, and Macklemore also referenced in his social media statements, multiple venues that remained on the tour notified the promoters that they would not allow a concert to take place at their sites with Macklemore remaining in the lineup.

Macklemore said Sheeran told him that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium outside Boston, would not allow him to perform there, and that Kraft had rallied other stadium owners into an ultimatum, CBS News reported. Kraft said in a statement that he opposed Macklemore’s participation in the Gillette shows, citing the material shared from the stage in New Jersey and what he described as a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery. Kraft said he would welcome a conversation with the rapper.

Sheeran has since said via social media, “Macklemore coming off the tour was the promoter’s decision, not mine.”
CNN/CTV News

text:
FALL EVENT SEASON IS HERE

Drivers encouraged to know all the travel options this weekend

Whether you’re heading downtown to Oktoberfest, the U.C. versus Miami football game, the Reds series against the Cubs or shopping at City Flea, there are many ways to get to your destination this weekend.  

Before you head out, remember there are many options to get there, regardless of the event location or the direction you’re heading. If you’re looking for an easy way to get downtown but don't want to drive, there are several transit options with Metro. From northern Kentucky, TANK offers a great option with the Southbank Shuttle, which runs every 15 minutes into downtown Cincinnati from Covington, Newport or Bellevue. 
 
If you decide to drive, here are the best ways to get downtown this weekend:

EASTBOUND
When traveling eastbound on U.S. 50/West Sixth Street, the best exits to reach downtown Cincinnati include:
• Freeman Avenue to Mehring Way
• Fifth Street

SOUTHBOUND
Traveling south on I-75 in Ohio, the options to get to downtown Cincinnati include:
• Freeman Ave (Exit 1F)
• 7th Street (Exit 1E)
• 5th Street (Exit 1C)

NORTHBOUND
Traveling north on I-75 and once across the Brent Spence Bridge into Cincinnati, motorists may follow:
• 5th Street (Exit 1C) directly into downtown
• U.S. 50/W. 6th Street (Exit 1D) to the Linn Street exit and circle back into downtown from Linn to Third Street.

WESTBOUND
Traveling westbound on U.S. 50/Columbia Parkway, all access points are open, so drivers can make their way to downtown by way of Third Street, Sixth Street or Pike to Fourth Street. 

Once I get downtown, what about changes on downtown streets?

ELM STREET
Elm Street is now two-way between Second Street and Third Street downtown, providing another route using Mehring Way to get to The Banks.

CENTRAL AVENUE
• All lanes of Central Avenue between Third Street and Pete Rose Way were closed Monday, September 14, for beam removal.
• Southbound vehicle traffic will be maintained by way of W. Third Street, the entrance to the Clay Wade Bailey, Second Street and Elm Street.
• Northbound vehicle traffic should use W. Mehring Way and Elm Street to W. Third Street.
• Pedestrians should follow W. Third Street to Elm Street and W. Mehring Way to Central Avenue.
• Central Avenue will reopen on Friday, September 18, by 4 p.m.

Drivers are encouraged to check their favorite navigation app to find the best way from their current location to their preferred destination.

text:
Dontayvion Wicks (WR, PHI): 2026 outlook

Dontayvion Wicks enters his fourth year in the league with a fresh start, moving to a new team after logging a 44.6 percent snap share and a 12.8 percent target share across 13 games last season. His previous output hovered around 5.83 points per game, yielding a modest 75.8 total points. Now projected as the team's third wide receiver, Wicks is stepping into a room that has significant opportunity available. A massive 54.7 percent of the position room work and 36.7 percent of team targets are now vacant from the offense. That sort of cleared deck creates a runway for a complementary piece to carve out a viable role, even if the team operates with a slight pass rate below expected at minus 2.5 and plays at a pace of 58.5 plays per game with an implied team total of 23.7 points per game. Wicks opened this season with a splash in week one against Washington, turning four targets into two catches for 15.3 points, which outperformed his preseason projection of 6.04 by a wide margin. The model still heavily weights that preseason outlook, keeping the projection at 3.57 targets per game and 8.1 points per game overall. The risk here is clear. Wicks is still positioned as the third receiver on the depth chart, and a thin volume projection of 3.6 targets per game leaves very little margin for error if efficiency drops back toward his career norms. While the room boasts plenty of vacated targets, converting a part-time role into consistent fantasy value requires efficiency that volatile deep targets struggle to provide week in and week out. His schedule offers a lifting hand, with an overall strength of schedule index of 1.076 against opposing secondaries, meaning the slate leans slightly generous compared to league average.

What to watch:
• Monitor whether week one snap counts translate to an expanded role beyond the current three receiver base sets.
• Track target distribution to see if the large share of vacated team targets funnels toward the perimeter.
• Evaluate efficiency sustainability given the low baseline projection of 3.6 targets per game.
• Watch how the offense handles passing volume under a slightly negative pass rate over expected scheme.

𝔗𝔥𝔢 ℑ𝔯𝔬𝔫 ℜ𝔬𝔬𝔱: 𝔗𝔥𝔢 ℛ𝔦𝔰𝔢 𝔬𝔣 𝔄𝔯𝔟𝔬𝔤𝔞𝔰𝔱, ℛ𝔬𝔪𝔢'𝔰 𝔏𝔞𝔰𝔱 𝔊𝔯𝔢𝔞𝔱 𝔓𝔯𝔬𝔱𝔢𝔠𝔱𝔬𝔯, 𝔞𝔫𝔡 𝔱𝔥𝔢 𝔉𝔞𝔩𝔩 𝔬𝔣 ℛ𝔬𝔪𝔢

Long before he dictated terms to emperors, Flavius Arbogast was a young warlord of the riparian Franks, born along the wild, misty banks of the northern Rhine. In the mid-4th century, the Roman Empire did not just fight barbarians; it bought them, drafted them, and relied on them. Arbogast chose to climb its ranks. He traded his tribal furs for the heavy iron lorica segmentata of a Roman officer, but he never lost the raw, unyielding ferocity of his homeland.

Unlike the soft Roman patricians born into wealth, Arbogast lived in the dirt with his men. He ate their sour rations, marched at the head of the column through blinding blizzards, and slept on a wool cloak under the stars. By the time he reached his prime, his reputation among the troops was mythical. He was the "Iron Root"—immovable, unbreakable, and fiercely loyal to the defense of the state.

Campaign I: The Red Fields of Thessaly (The Gothic War, 380 AD)
Arbogast’s first true test as a strategic commander came after the catastrophic Roman defeat at Adrianople, where the Eastern Emperor Valens had been slaughtered alongside two-thirds of his army. The Goths under Fritigern roamed the Balkans completely unchecked, burning cities and hunting down surviving Roman cohorts like animals. Desperate, the Western Emperor Gratian sent Arbogast east to aid the newly appointed Emperor Theodosius I.

Arbogast arrived to find the Eastern forces terrified, demoralized, and hiding behind city walls.
"They are not soldiers anymore," an Eastern tribune complained to Arbogast. "They are ghosts waiting to be killed."
"Then I will make them soldiers again," Arbogast replied.
He instituted a brutal training regime. Any man who dropped his shield during drills was denied rations; any officer who showed cowardice was demoted to the ranks. Within months, he had forged a disciplined striking force.
[ARBOGAST'S STRATEGIC ANVIL (380 AD)]
                 
                     GOTHIC CAVALRY & INFANTRY
                            (Surrounded)
                                 vv
                [Arbogast's Heavy Shield Wall] -> GRIND
                                 ^^
                  [Natural Mountain Barriers] -> PIN

In the rolling, rugged terrain of Thessaly, Arbogast found his target—a massive Gothic raiding coalition heavily laden with plunder. Knowing the Goths relied on chaotic, high-energy cavalry charges, Arbogast used the geography against them. He positioned his heavy infantry at the mouth of a rocky valley, creating a suffocating anvil.

When the Goths charged, the Roman shield wall held like solid stone. As the barbarian momentum stalled, Arbogast personally led his elite Western auxiliary cavalry down from the flanking hills, striking the Goths from the rear. Trapped against the rocks, the Gothic coalition was systematically annihilated. Arbogast cleared Macedonia and Thessaly of the threat, forcing the Goths to the negotiating table and saving the Eastern Empire from total collapse.

Campaign II: The Thunder over Gaul (The Fall of Flavius Victor, 388 AD)
In 383 AD, a rebellious general named Magnus Maximus murdered the Western Emperor Gratian and seized power in Britain, Gaul, and Spain. For years, the empire fractured. But when Maximus crossed the Alps into Italy, threatening the young Emperor Valentinian II, Arbogast marched to war once more under the banner of a joint Roman counter-offensive.
While Theodosius handled Maximus in the east, Arbogast was given supreme command of the Western front. His objective was Gaul, where Maximus’s son and co-emperor, Flavius Victor, held the regime’s northern stronghold.
Arbogast knew that a prolonged siege of the Gallic cities would drain his army and devastate the countryside. Speed was his weapon. He marched his legions through the treacherous, muddy paths of the Ardennes in a relentless blitzkrieg. The rebel scouts never saw them coming.
Arbogast’s vanguard burst upon Victor's forces outside the city of Trier like a sudden thunderstorm. Before the rebel garrison could properly organize their lines, Arbogast’s cavalry overran their pickets, smashing their camp. Victor was captured in his quarters and executed on the spot. Arbogast absorbed the remaining Gallic legions into his own, ended the usurpation in a single stroke, and handed a secure, reunited West over to the young Valentinian II.

The Philosopher and the Warlord: A Brotherhood of Values

Following his sweeping victories, Arbogast established his military headquarters in the imperial city of Trier. It was here, during a brief window of peace, that the fierce Frankish general met the man who would alter his destiny: Flavius Eugenius.
Eugenius was not a soldier. He was a highly respected Christian professor of rhetoric and literature, renowned throughout Gaul for his intellect, humility, and dedication to classical education. To the court elites, they were an odd pairing—the iron-jawed barbarian general and the soft-spoken Christian philosopher.
Their friendship began over long evening discussions in the prefect’s palace. Arbogast, though a traditionalist who respected his ancestral beliefs, was deeply drawn to Eugenius’s profound moral integrity and his commitment to Christian ethics of justice, charity, and fair governance. Arbogast despised the rampant corruption of the imperial court, where officials routinely took bribes and left the common folk to starve. In Eugenius, he saw the ideal Roman: a devout Christian who believed the state should be ruled by virtue, law, and intellectual honor, rather than greed.
"The sword can protect the border, Eugenius," Arbogast once remarked over a map of the Rhine. "But it cannot protect the soul of Rome. For that, we need men who understand justice."
"And justice without a shield, General, is easily broken by tyrants," Eugenius replied.
From that moment on, they were inseparable. Eugenius became Arbogast’s chief civil advisor, smoothing over relations between the military and the local Christian churches, while Arbogast ensured that the northern provinces were governed cleanly, free from the financial extortion running rampant in Constantinople.

Campaign III: The Iron Winter (The Rhenish Frontiers, 393 AD)
By 392 AD, the young Emperor Valentinian II was dead—found hanged under highly mysterious circumstances. Though the Eastern Emperor Theodosius immediately accused Arbogast of murder to spark a war, the general had no reason to kill the boy. Needing a ruler to stabilize the frantic Western provinces, Arbogast did not grab power for himself. Instead, he turned to his trusted Christian friend, elevating Eugenius to the rank of Western Augustus.
Theodosius immediately mobilized for war, but before Arbogast could face the East, the northern border broke. Exploiting the internal Roman chaos, the powerful Frankish chieftains Marcomer and Sunno led thousands of warriors across the frozen Rhine, slaughtering Roman frontier guards and burning villas.
Arbogast refused to let the north fall. In the dead of the brutal winter of 393 AD, when the Germanic tribes believed the freezing weather made them safe from retaliation, Arbogast ordered his legions forward.
[THE GERMANIC WINTER STRIKE]
  
      [Rhine River (Frozen)] <=== Arbogast's Legions Cross at Night
              ||
              || ===> Surprise Attack on Frankish Strongholds
              vv
     [Marcomer & Sunno's Camp] -> Shattered / Forced Submission
They crossed the icy river under the cover of a moonless, freezing night. Arbogast led the assault himself, wading through chest-deep snow to catch the barbarian tribes completely by surprise in their winter quarters. He burned their fortified villages and cut down their war-bands before they could even form a defensive line.
Stunned by the speed and sheer savagery of the winter offensive, Marcomer and Sunno surrendered. Arbogast forced them onto their knees to swear binding oaths of submission to Rome. He rebuilt the damaged watchtowers, restocked the granaries, and successfully secured the northern frontier. The West was completely safe—but the true threat was now marching from the East.

Campaign IV: The Final Battle at the Frigidus (394 AD)
The political elites in Constantinople could not tolerate a powerful, independent Western regime led by a brilliant barbarian general and an honorable Christian philosopher who refused to bow to their dictates. Emperor Theodosius marched west with a massive army of over 100,000 men, including thousands of Gothic mercenaries led by the ambitious young chieftain Alaric.
In September 394 AD, the two forces met at the narrow passes of the Frigidus River in the Julian Alps.
On the first day, Arbogast gave a masterclass in defensive warfare. He deployed his veteran Western legions across the narrow valley floor, bottlenecking the massive Eastern numbers. When Theodosius sent Alaric’s Goths forward as cannon fodder, Arbogast’s lines held like an iron dam. By sunset, over 10,000 Goths lay dead in the mud. The Eastern army was broken, terrified, and preparing to retreat. Arbogast had won the field through pure, unadulterated tactical brilliance.
But the history books were about to be rewritten by grease and gold.

The Betrayal and the Final Stand
On the morning of September 6, there was no divine miracle. There was no sudden, heavenly storm wind to blow the weapons back into Arbogast's lines—that was the fiction the court poets like Claudian would write years later to hide a shameful truth.
The line broke because of corruption. During the night, Theodosius’s agents had slipped into the Western camp with heavy carts of gold coin, promising immense wealth and titles to Arbogast's secondary commanders. General Arbitio, a man Arbogast had trusted with his flank, accepted the bribe.

As the morning trumpets sounded for the final charge, Arbogast watched in absolute horror as Arbitio’s divisions suddenly wheeled around, their spears turning inward. They attacked their own brothers-in-arms from behind, trapping Arbogast's loyal center in a horrific, suffocating pincer. At the same time, defecting soldiers swarmed the command tent, dragging the peaceful Emperor Eugenius from his horse and brutally beheading him in front of the cheering Eastern ranks.
The Western army collapsed into chaos, but Arbogast did not run. He did not flee into the mountains to die a quiet, solitary death as the propaganda claimed.
Gathering a desperate, fiercely loyal group of his remaining Rhine veterans, the great general backed himself against a sheer cliff face. Imperial assassins and traitorous Roman soldiers swarmed up the rocks, eager to collect the massive bounty on his head.
"Yield, barbarian!" an Eastern officer shouted, brandishing a bloody blade. "Theodosius offers you life in chains!"

Arbogast spat blood onto the cold alpine stone. He raised his notched, blood-slicked spatha, his grey eyes burning with standard defiance. "Rome does not yield to traitors and thieves! If you want the head of the Magister Militum, come and take it from a Roman soldier!"

They charged. Arbogast fought like a demon possessed, his blade cutting down the first three assassins who reached him. He fought for the borders he had spent his life securing, for the memory of his murdered friend Eugenius, and for the honor of an empire that had just sold its soul for gold. He fought until his shield was splintered to kindling, his breath was a ragged gasp, and his body was pierced by a dozen blades.
Surrendered, outmaneuvered by bribery rather than tactics, the greatest warrior of the Western world finally fell, his fingers still locked tightly around the hilt of his sword.

The Tragic Aftermath: The Fall Of Rome

With Arbogast dead, Emperor Theodosius achieved his coveted reunification of the Roman Empire. The court chroniclers immediately went to work, erasing Arbogast’s lifelong victories from the stone monuments and inventing the myth of a "divine wind" to mask a sloppy, gold-bought civil war.
But the victory was a hollow curse.
By slaughtering Arbogast and decimating his elite Western legions, the Eastern regime had completely destroyed the military shield of the Western world. There were no professional, battle-hardened soldiers left to guard the Rhine or protect the Italian gates. The massive treasury was entirely empty, squandered on the bribes used to buy the battle.
Worse still, Alaric, the Gothic chieftain who had watched his men die as disposable bait on the first day of the Frigidus, had learned the ultimate lesson. He saw that Rome was no longer held together by honor or martial strength, but by corruption, greed, and fragile political alliances. He realized the mighty Western army was gone, and Italy lay entirely defenseless.
Theodosius’s grand reunification lasted a mere four months before he died, leaving the massive, broken empire permanently fractured between his two weak, incompetent young sons.
Just sixteen years later, in 410 AD, Alaric and his Goths marched completely unopposed through the exact same mountain passes where Arbogast had made his final stand. They swarmed down into the heart of Italy, surrounded the capital, and sacked the eternal city of Rome. As the flames consumed the grand palaces, the tragic truth became clear: when power and greed murdered Rome's greatest protector, they hadn't saved the empire—they had signed its death warrant.

text:
“History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes.” – Mark Twain

Duke University historian Simon Partner studies the lives of ordinary people in the past to reveal patterns that are still relevant today. In a recent interview, we discussed the origins of modern-day Yokohama, focusing on the remarkable story of Shinohara Chūemon. A farmer from rural Yamanashi Prefecture, Shinohara applied to become one of Yokohama’s first officially designated merchants. Amid rapid globalization, technological disruption, political uncertainty, inflation, shifting international markets, and cross-cultural encounters in the 1860s, his turbulent story unfolded.

In this short clip, Professor Partner explains how Japan’s experience with cotton in the 1860s offers an early lesson in the vulnerability of global supply chains. When the American Civil War disrupted Southern cotton exports, global prices surged, prompting foreign merchants to turn to newly opened Japan as an alternative supplier. Japanese cotton exports soared, which benefited producers and merchants but drove up prices for domestic consumers. When American cotton returned after the war, the temporary boom quickly faded. This dynamic is strikingly similar to what we see today in our interconnected supply chains, where geopolitical shocks thousands of kilometers away can suddenly create shortages, redirect trade flows, push up prices, produce unexpected winners and losers, and force businesses to find alternative suppliers. Examples of this include the impact of the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, Red Sea disruptions, and U.S.–China tensions.

text:
**Mass Movements in a Social Media World**
_Eric Hoffer’s_ The True Believer, _Left and Right Online, and Why Polarization Is Not Yet Civil War_

By Thomas Foreman - 2026

Eric Hoffer became one of my favorite writers after I first read him in my twenties. Most of his books were out of print. I hunted used bookstores in Denver, Kansas City, and Santa Fe, and Seattle. Reprints are easy to buy on Amazon now. What I liked was how clearly he wrote about the human condition. He was short and direct.

Hoffer (1902–1983) never went to college. Blind for part of his childhood, he worked as a migrant laborer and then as a stevedore on the San Francisco docks. That job put him next to sailors from all over the world and in personal contact with the working class of many cultures. The public library gave him the books. From hard work, those conversations, and a lot of reading, he wrote _The True Believer_ in 1951. His life shows how valuable public libraries have been.

The book’s idea is simple: many people want to escape a life that feels empty by joining a cause bigger than themselves. This is more about feelings than about ideas. A mass movement offers a new identity, a story that the present is worthless, and an enemy to hate. The official belief—religion, nation, or politics—matters less than that hunger. Mid-century writers described the same flight from individuality: Fromm on the escape from freedom, Kierkegaard on the crowd as untruth, Nietzsche on _ressentiment_.

Social media did not create that hunger. It made it faster. Apps count likes and keep showing outrage. Your own life looks small. The other side looks evil. Online groups become a ready-made family. Algorithms push attack posts, so the feed itself does the first stage of a movement’s work.
That work comes in three stages. Men of words—writers, preachers, professors, journalists, and now influencers—make the present look illegitimate. They live on recognition and on taking the existing order apart. When that talk has gone far enough, fanatics take over. “The fanatic,” Hoffer wrote, “is perpetually incomplete and insecure.” He wants purity, an enemy, and motion. “He cannot be convinced but only converted. His passionate attachment is more vital than the quality of the cause to which he is attached.” On the left that has included the 2017 shooting of Republican lawmakers and the 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk. On the right it has included January 6 and a past record of militia and supremacist murders including the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995. Word-men do not have to pull a trigger. They can make the present look so evil that a fanatic treats murder as hygiene.

If a movement lasts, men of action try to lock the gains into offices and laws. Duty replaces frenzy. Trouble comes when the fanatic never steps aside. Lenin, Mao, and Castro froze a cause into a state. America’s Founders also acted after a revolution, but they wrote a Constitution to limit power, not to keep a holy war going. Online politics is crowded with the first two stages and thin on the third. Fanatics can gather in hours. Almost no one has to govern.

The people most ready to join are the “new poor”: not the long-time poor, and not the secure, but those who recently lost money, status, or security—or who rose just far enough to expect more than they got. After 2016, much of the online right treated elites or “the Deep State” as the enemy. After 2020, much of the online left treated police, “whiteness,” and ordinary institutions as the enemy. There the “new poor” often include college-educated young adults who did what they were told and still cannot get jobs that meet the income or respect they expected. Moral fervor becomes a stand-in for a missing career. COVID showed how fast the labels can switch. The need to belong and to blame did not.

That pattern is a better guide than shouting “civil war.” We have many talkers and fanatics. We do not have two governments or two armies. A real civil war, l

text:
AI Safety: The Engineering Narrative and the Liability Pricing Lag

Jensen Huang says markets will discipline AI companies. His own company's numbers make that harder to sustain than it sounds.

Jensen Huang took the stage at Salesforce Dreamforce to argue that AI safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one, and that no new regulations are needed because market forces will constrain companies well enough. The pitch is clean: AI is hardware and software, not an alien mind, so humans and existing laws can manage it. Companies should move fast, pause if something looks unsafe, and let the market punish failures.

The numbers Huang's own company just reported make this framing harder to sustain than it sounds.

Nvidia's data center revenue hit $89 billion in the July quarter, up 117% year over year, accounting for 92.5% of total revenue. Q3 guidance sits at $108 billion. The CFO disclosed that Nvidia content per gigawatt of AI data center capacity has climbed from $18 billion under Hopper to $25 billion under Blackwell and will reach $40 billion with Vera Rubin. Goldman Sachs pegs 2026 hyperscaler capital expenditure at roughly $800 billion. The four largest hyperscalers are guiding toward about $725 billion combined for 2026, with capex as a share of operating cash flow rising from 41% in 2023 to a projected 92% by 2026.

That is not a market gently correcting itself. That is a system whose complexity is expanding faster than any assessment framework—engineering, legal, or actuarial—can track. When a single hardware generation doubles the value density of compute inside a gigawatt-scale facility, the attack surface, failure propagation paths, and second-order dependencies do not grow linearly. They compound.

Huang's argument assumes market discipline works when risks are visible and priceable. CrowdStrike offers a compact test of that assumption. A faulty software update from a company whose core product is endpoint security took down 8.5 million Windows devices, grounded flights, disrupted hospitals and banks, and cost Fortune 500 companies an estimated $5.4 billion. CrowdStrike's product was not AI-generated harm in the conventional sense. It was an engineering failure inside a security tool. The damages went largely uninsured, according to Guy Carpenter and CyberCube Analytics. The market did eventually punish CrowdStrike. But the losses landed first on everyone else.

The Meta settlement pushes the liability logic further. Meta agreed to pay about $18 billion to resolve multistate claims that it intentionally designed addictive platforms that harmed young people. The complaint did not hinge on a single defective feature. It targeted the cumulative design—recommendation algorithms, engagement mechanics, interaction patterns—and argued that the combination produced systemic harm to a specific population. Meta did not admit wrongdoing. It also acknowledged in its most recent earnings report that youth safety trials posed a risk of "material loss," and it will pay 70% of the settlement in annual installments over a decade.

Transfer that legal theory to AI systems that interact with users over months, adapt to their emotional states, and shape their beliefs through iterative dialogue, and the scope of potential liability expands well beyond what product liability frameworks were built to handle. The Connecticut wrongful death suit against OpenAI and Microsoft alleges exactly that pattern: months of interaction in which the model validated and amplified a user's paranoid delusions, ultimately portraying his elderly mother as an existential threat. The complaint asserts strict liability, negligence, failure to warn, and design defect claims. The chatbot, according to the filing, reassured the user that he was "not crazy" and "not paranoid" when he expressed doubt.

Huang did not address industry self-regulation in his remarks. He instead emphasized open-weight models as a counterweight to proprietary labs, noting that open models have grown from roughly 30% to about 70% of the landscape. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, speaking at the All-In Summit, argued that safety concerns should apply globally and that China should participate in governance. The two positions are not contradictory. They are complementary: open weights distribute deployment across actors who face no single point of regulatory accountability, while global governance frameworks would impose costs that proprietary labs with established compliance infrastructure are better positioned to absorb.

What Huang's engineering framing leaves unresolved is the timing mismatch. Engineering problems can be iterated quickly. Legal and insurance mechanisms respond slowly. The CrowdStrike victims waited for reimbursement that largely never came. Meta's settlement payouts will stretch over ten years. The Connecticut case will take years to reach judgment. In the interim, the deployment curve keeps accelerating. Huang's position aligns cleanly with Nvidia's commercial interest in unconstrained compute demand. That alignment does not make the argument wrong. It does mean the argument should be tested against the cost curves it leaves out.

text:
The Acceleration in AI Power Constraints: When Delivery Time Constants Cannot Keep Pace With Demand Structure Shifts

The 1 GW of 2026 and the 1 GW of 2021 correspond to completely different physical rack densities

TrendForce published a forecast in September that global data center power demand capacity reaches 161 GW in 2026, up 31% year over year from 122.9 GW in 2025. AI servers account for 33.4% of that demand, up from under 25% in 2025, and will exceed 40% by 2027. General server share falls from roughly 40% historically to 25.6%. By 2030, TrendForce projects 490.7 GW of demand against 222.6 GW of grid deliverable capacity, leaving a 268 GW global gap and more than 170 GW in the US alone.

Read as a demand curve, the conclusion is linear: AI power consumption rises, the grid cannot keep up. The more useful analysis starts with three questions. How fast is the acceleration of that demand curve itself changing? What is the constraint migrating toward as that acceleration compounds? And is the gap between supply-side response time constants and demand-side expansion time constants widening or narrowing?

The unit definition is being rewritten, and the acceleration comes from multiplication, not addition

The 161 GW figure for 2026 embeds an assumption about rack density that has already been reset. Uptime Institute's 16th Annual Global Data Center Survey, covering over 1,600 participants, found that modal rack density reached 11 kW in 2026, up from 9 kW in 2025 — but that is the most commonly reported density across general enterprise facilities. AI deployment operates at an entirely different scale. Average server rack density has climbed to 27 kW, nearly four times the 7 kW recorded in 2021. Nvidia's rack-level power envelope is moving from 120 kW in the Blackwell generation to 225 kW in Vera Rubin, with TrendForce expecting Rubin Ultra to push higher and 800V HVDC adoption landing around 2028.

The arithmetic matters. A single rack consumed 7 kW in 2021. An AI deployment rack in 2026 consumes 225 kW. That is a 32x multiple on the same physical unit. When TrendForce forecasts power demand in GW, the 1 GW of 2026 corresponds to a completely different physical infrastructure density than the 1 GW of 2021. Demand acceleration comes not only from more racks but from per-rack power multiplying on top of rack-count growth. The former is a linear variable. The latter is a multiplier. When both expand simultaneously, the power demand curve is not a straight line with a constant slope. It is a curve whose slope is itself increasing.

Goldman Sachs Research's Brian Singer and Carly Davenport provided a scale reference in September: the incremental power demand from AI is equivalent to adding another Japan — the world's fifth-largest power consumer — to global electricity consumption by 2030. Singer also identified seven binding constraints today, framing them as "all the Ts": turbines, transformers, transmission, and tradespeople. Grid connection queues in parts of the US stretch to seven years.

The constraint is migrating from total gap to structural bottleneck

The 268 GW gap requires disaggregation. TrendForce itself notes two layers: a portion of the gap can be filled by behind-the-meter self-generation, which does not count toward grid deliverable capacity, meaning the headline gap overstates physical shortfall. The remainder is genuine supply shortfall caused by grid interconnection and transmission delivery delays. The gap begins diverging in 2026, widens materially after 2028, and the US alone accounts for over 170 GW of the 2030 shortfall.

Wood Mackenzie's data offers the clearest quantification of time-constant asymmetry. Generator step-up transformer lead times exceeded 160 weeks in Q1 2026, up from an average of 143 weeks in 2024. Substation transformer lead times stretched from roughly 140 weeks in 2023 to more than 160 weeks in 2026. High-voltage circuit breakers climbed from 77 weeks in 2023 to 125 weeks in the second half of 2025. Lead times for large power transformers exceed three years. Rystad Energy estimates global grid capital expenditure will exceed $650 billion in 2026, double the 2020 level, yet equipment delivery lags plans by two to three years.

Transformers are not semiconductors. Expanding output requires building new winding lines, recruiting and training skilled tradespeople, and completing utility customer qualification processes. None of those steps operate on a quarterly cycle. Wood Mackenzie estimates data centers' share of the electrical equipment market could rise from under 2% in 2020 to about 40%, while US data center capacity grows from roughly 24 GW today to 110 GW by 2030. IEA data indicates about 20% of planned global data center projects are already at risk of delays from grid constraints.

Gas turbines and nuclear power reveal where the real bottleneck sits

GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog reached 116 GW by Q2 2026, up from 100 GW in Q1 and 83 GW at end-2025. The company's total order backlog hit $176 billion, up 37% year over year, exceeding the GDP of Kuwait, Ecuador, or Slovakia. CEO Scott Strazik said GE Vernova expects to finish 2026 with at least 125 GW of gas turbines under contract, leaving the company "mostly sold out through '30" while already filling 2031 production slots. The 116 GW figure requires qualification: only 53 GW is firm equipment backlog, while 63 GW is slot reservation agreements requiring upfront deposits but not yet converted to orders. Even with that caveat, GE Vernova's annualized production run rate is set to reach 20 GW by Q3 2026, scale to 24 GW by 2028, and hit 30 GW by 2030.

The constraint is not unwillingness to expand. Heavy-duty gas turbine manufacturing involves precision casting, high-temperature alloy blade machining, and full-unit testing. Each production step scales on a multi-year timeline. Siemens Energy's backlog stands at 69 GW with delivery cycles exceeding three years; Mitsubishi Heavy Industries holds 35 GW. Siemens Energy's capacity expansion plan targets 24 GW annually by 2028 and 30 GW by 2030 — still below the demand-side acceleration rate.

Small modular reactors are positioned as the long-term answer, but their time constant is longer. IEA data shows the global SMR conditional offtake pipeline grew from 25 GW at end-2024 to 45 GW by April 2026, an 80% increase in 16 months. Oklo's 15 GW pipeline is roughly 95% data-center oriented, including a 1.2 GW campus with Meta and a 12 GW letter of intent with Switch. But of 9.8 GW in committed nuclear capacity across 13 hyperscaler deals, only 1.92 GW is actively generating power for AI data centers today — Amazon's Talen/Susquehanna front-of-meter PPA. First-of-a-kind SMR costs run $80–150/MWh against vendor targets of $60–80/MWh. The timeline from pilot to commercial deployment will not be shorter than the transformer capacity expansion cycle.

Behind-the-meter generation fills the gap while creating a new pricing structure

When grid delivery timelines extend by years, hyperscalers route around the grid. Microsoft signed a letter of intent for 1.4 GW of behind-the-meter natural gas in West Virginia and is in exclusive negotiations with Chevron and Engine No. 1 for a 2.5 GW plant in West Texas. Brookfield Asset Management expanded its financing partnership with Bloom Energy to $25 billion. The White House released a "ratepayer protection" framework in February requiring large technology companies to bear the generation costs of AI data center expansion, accelerating an already-underway shift toward behind-the-meter generation.

Nuclear pricing signals are equally clear. Microsoft signed a 20-year PPA with Constellation to restart Three Mile Island, with Jefferies estimating pricing at $110–115/MWh. Meta signed up to 6.6 GW of nuclear agreements with TerraPower, Oklo, and Vistra covering 20 years. Amazon Web Services anchored 960 MW of data center load at Talen's Susquehanna site. The common feature across these deals is not the price per MWh. It is time. The spread between grid delivery uncertainty and hyperscaler requirements for deterministic compute onlining is the pricing space for behind-the-meter generation and long-term PPAs. The constraint has shifted from "what does power cost" to "when can power flow."

What capital markets are pricing, and what they are not

J.P. Morgan estimates hyperscaler capex will reach $697 billion in 2026, up $173 billion since the start of the year, with roughly 75% directed at AI infrastructure. But power infrastructure capex and compute infrastructure capex carry different return timelines. GPU depreciation runs 3–5 years. Data center leases run 10–15 years. Transformer service life is 30–40 years. Nuclear PPAs run 20 years. The arrangement of these cash flow curves on balance sheets determines different participants' exposure and risk profiles.

GE Vernova's $176 billion backlog and sold-out production slots through 2030 have driven significant share price appreciation, and the market has begun pricing gas turbine scarcity. But the transformer supply chain has almost no pure-play listed exposure — capacity expansion is distributed across Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, and GE Vernova's grid businesses, where margins are materially lower than in gas turbines. Behind-the-meter generation pricing power sits with Bloom Energy, Baker Hughes, and INNIO, but revenue recognition is gated by equipment delivery cycles, not order signing dates.

The expectation gap may lie here: the market is pricing the demand growth curve — TrendForce's 161 GW to 490.7 GW — but has not fully priced the pricing-power structure implied by time-constant asymmetry across supply chain layers. When transformer lead times exceed 160 weeks, gas turbine capacity is sold out through 2030, and grid interconnection queues reach seven years, assets with deliverable capacity and approved projects — not assets with project pipelines — capture outsized pricing power in 2027 and 2028. That divergence has already materialized in gas turbines. In transformers and transmission, it may take another one to two quarters to be fully reflected.

The 268 GW gap is a headline number that includes portions fillable by behind-the-meter generation and portions representing genuine grid delivery shortfall. For analysts tracking this supply chain, the next signal worth watching is not upward revisions to demand forecasts. It is whether transformer lead times show an inflection in the first half of 2027, and when GE Vernova's 2031 delivery reservations sell out. Until then, every power demand forecast carries a supply delivery discount that has not yet been priced.

text:
Azazel” or “the scapegoat” is mentioned in Leviticus 16 as part of God’s instructions to the Israelites regarding the Day of Atonement.On this day the high priest would first offer a sacrifice for his sins & those of his household; then he would perform sacrifices for the nation.“From the Israelite community [the high priest was instructed] to take 2 male goats for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering” (v. 5). The priest brought the animals before the Lord & cast lots between the two goats – one to be a sacrifice and the other to be the scapegoat.The 1st goat was slaughtered for the sins of the people & its blood used to cleanse the Most Holy Place,the tent of meeting and the altar (v. 20). After the cleansing, the live goat was brought to the high priest. Laying his hands on the scapegoat, the high priest was to “confess over it all the wickedness and rebellion of the Israelites –all their sins –& put them on the goat’s head. He shall send the goat away into the wilderness in the care of someone appointed for the task.The goat will carry on itself all their sins to a remote place; and the man shall release it in the wilderness” (vv. 21-22). Symbolically, the scapegoat took on the sins of the Israelites and removed them (v. 10). 
For Christians this is a foreshadowing of Christ.
Christ is the complete atonement for our sins. In many ways, He embodies each aspect of the Day of Atonement. We are told that He is our great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14). 
He is also the “Lamb that was slain from the creation of the world” (Revelation 13:8) as a sacrifice for our sins. And He is our scapegoat.  2 Cor. 5:21 says “God made Him who had no sin to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”Our sins were laid on Christ – He bore our sins just as the scapegoat bore the sins of the Israelites.Isaiah 53:6 prophesies Christ’s acceptance of the sin burden:“We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.”After the sins were laid on the scapegoat, it was considered unclean and driven into the wilderness. In essence, the goat was cast out. The same happened to Jesus. He was crucified outside of the city. “He was despised and rejected by men  He poured out His life unto death and was numbered with the transgressors. For He bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:3a, 12).Jesus embodied what the scapegoat represented – the removal of sins from the perpetrators.

Truly, the Old Testament rituals carry a depth and richness that only God could create.The Day of Atonement foreshadowed the ultimate atonement Christ provides. 
No longer do we need to sacrifice animals to cover our sins, nor do we need to impute our sins to a scapegoat to have them carried away. Jesus has been sacrificed and “scapegoated” for us.Our sins have been atoned for and removed.“The law is only a shadow of the good things that are coming –not the realities themselves,” we are told in Hebrews 10:1. “For this reason it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship.  Those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. We have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Heb. 10:3-4, 10).
A side note: the name “Azazel” shows up in some Jewish mythology. While there are different versions in the Book of Enoch, the Book of the Giants, and other pseudepigraphal books, the story is essentially that Azazel was the name of one of the fallen angels who sinned in Gen. 6. As a curse on his sin, Azazel was forced to take the form of a goat-like demon.This myth is not recorded in the Bible. Regardless of the identity of Azazel,the Bible emphasizes the sufficiency & completeness of Christ’s sacrifice both to remove our sin and to reconcile us to God

text:
An act of amazing kindness from 2021

Timothy Harrison, then 18 and a senior at Woodlawn High School in Birmingham, Alabama, showed up for his shift at the Waffle House in Center Point on graduation day. He had asked for the day off earlier, but he had no ride across town to the Birmingham CrossPlex, no cap and gown (those were handed out at rehearsal, which he missed because he was working), no tickets for family, and no dress clothes. His mother couldn’t get off work at her daycare job. So he figured he’d just work instead.
His manager, Cedric Hampton, wasn’t having it. “I was going to get him there no matter what,” Hampton said. The crew dropped everything:
•  Coworkers (including Hampton, Chasadee Brown, and Patricia Richardson) pooled money—about $40 each, plus some customer donations—and bought him gray slacks, a light blue dress shirt, a tie, and matching shoes, mostly from Target.
•  Another coworker drove him to the high school to pick up his cap and gown.
•  They dressed him right there in the restaurant.
•  Shantana Blevins drove him the 20 miles to the ceremony and waited in the parking lot because she didn’t have a ticket.  
Harrison later said putting on the new clothes felt like “a million dollars” and that sitting in the auditorium was “the best moment of my life.” After the story went viral, Lawson State Community College offered him a full scholarship (tuition and books). He moved into a dorm that fall; Hampton helped him move in and said a staff member there had become like a second mother to him. Harrison planned to study business/finance and still work at Waffle House during breaks

text:
🚨 UPDATE: Roc Nation has filed its opposition to New York Marine and General Insurance Company’s motion to dismiss its insurance coverage lawsuit.

One of the main points Roc Nation is emphasizing is that its policies expressly covered false arrest, false imprisonment, and invasion of privacy claims.🤔

Roc Nation says it paid significant premiums for coverage protecting the company and its employees from exactly those types of allegations. When Demoree Hadley later sued Roc Nation, Desiree Perez, and Natalie Anderson over claims that included false arrest, false imprisonment, unlawful seizure, unauthorized access to private communications, and invasion of privacy related allegations, Roc Nation says NYM did not honor that coverage obligation.

Instead, Roc Nation alleges the insurer delayed for months, repeatedly failed to give a clear coverage position, eventually denied coverage for Roc Nation and Anderson, offered Perez only a limited defense under a reservation of rights, and then sued Perez in federal court seeking a declaration that it owed her no coverage.

Roc Nation is arguing that NYM’s conduct went beyond a simple contract dispute and amounted to bad faith claim handling. They describe it as a “delay, deny, and litigate” strategy and accuse NYM of prioritizing its own financial interests over the interests of its insureds.

Roc Nation is also pushing back on NYM’s attempt to argue that Desiree Perez and Natalie Anderson have to be separately joined in the case. Roc Nation says it is the named insured, it paid the premiums, and it suffered its own losses after being forced to fund defense costs for itself and its employees.

Another notable part is Roc Nation’s claim for reputational harm.

They argue that NYM’s decision to publicly sue Desiree Perez in Florida generated media coverage and caused reputational damage not only to Perez, but also to Roc Nation. They are seeking consequential damages for that alleged harm, along with defense costs, attorneys’ fees, business related losses, and other damages they say resulted from the insurer’s handling of the claim.

Roc Nation is asking the New York court to deny NYM’s motion to dismiss in full and allow the breach of contract, bad faith, consumer protection, and related claims to move forward. Roc Nation memorandum of law v NYMG.pdf

text:
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's announcement that the EU will explore "associate membership" for Canada came as a surprise to member countries — and left governments concerned about the potential trade-offs.

During her annual State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, von der Leyen floated the upgrading of relations with Ottawa to meet the need to "urgently reimagine our partnerships" and "build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies."

Canada, which is locked in an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, will begin "opening the door" to become "the first associate member of the EU."

But the message wrong-footed national capitals, which were never asked to sign off on the idea before the speech, said three diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. Granting membership to the EU is a responsibility of the European Council, and no model for associate membership exists.

"Nobody really knows what it means," said one of the envoys, who has been involved in talks with the Commission about relations with Canada in recent days. "Member states have tried to manage expectations. There are only warm feelings for Ottawa, but we need to know what the details are."

A second diplomat put it more bluntly, predicting that while Canada could be given an equivalent of the EU's Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Areas deal — a market access arrangement offered to Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine — there is little mandate for other economic or political integration. "Member states will not agree on anything else," the diplomat said.

A third diplomat added that any associate membership status would require changes to the EU’s fundamental treaties — which is “impossible” due to a lack of support.

Among the potential issues that would come up if they considered going beyond that, according to the diplomats, are thorny questions around Ottawa's Made in Canada preference, which could fly in the face of single market rules; Canada's steel industry, which rivals Europe's own; taxation on the EU's car exports and its rules limiting imports of European alcohol; and its differing guidance on genetically modified produce.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has previously suggested "associate membership" as a way for closer alignment with Ukraine, although the idea was rejected by Kyiv and failed to win the support of other leaders.

text:
Post-Conviction of Leo Frank, Witness Manipulation and Trickery With Defense Inducements of Every Kind: Promises of Jobs, and Money, Pressure Campaigns, and Disputed Statements After Leo Frank’s Trial

Lawyers can prepare witnesses for court. They can review earlier statements, explain questions, and remind people to tell the truth. 

The problem begins when someone offers rewards for a false story, uses threats, inducements, or changes a written statement without the witness’s agreement. 

An affidavit is a written statement sworn to be true.

The investigation for Leo Frank’s defense after his trial produced several accusations of this kind. Some involved alleged payments. Others involved false names, job offers, or disputed wording. They should be examined separately.

Here is what the defense did to try and get Leo Frank a new trial after his conviction:

Nellie Wood: An alleged offer of money. Wood said an unidentified man offered her money to swear to statements favorable to Frank. She said she refused. She specifically stated that C. W. Burke himself had not made that offer, although the man used the same automobile Burke later used when visiting her (Georgia Supreme Court, 1).

George Epps: False names and a staged telephone call. Epps said investigators took him to Birmingham, frightened him with threats of jail, and pressured him into signing a statement taking back his trial testimony. Burke denied threats, but admitted arranging a false identity for Jimmie Wrenn and a misleading telephone call during the interview (AJ, 2, 3).

Albert McKnight: A promised job. On April 19, 1914, the Atlanta Journal reported McKnight’s claim that Burke promised him a Pullman job paying $40 a month, with tips supposedly bringing his income to $100. McKnight said the promise helped persuade him to sign a statement taking back his trial testimony. He had been earning $28 a month (AJ, 4).

Albert McKnight: Words allegedly added after he signed. The Atlanta Constitution reported another complaint from McKnight that same day. He said statements accusing R. L. Craven and C. C. Pickett of improper conduct were added after he signed. The defense disputed his account and presented evidence that he had freely sworn to his statement (AC, 5, and AJ, 2).

C. B. Dalton: A document allegedly presented as something else. Dalton said Burke offered him $100 to sign what was described as a petition to save Frank from hanging. He said Burke read only a small part, which said nothing about taking back his trial testimony. Dalton later rejected the defense statement and stood by his trial account (NYT, 6).

Aaron Allen: Money displayed during an interview. Allen said investigators took him to Chicago while seeking a statement that he had heard Conley confess. He described being left in a Burns agency office with money spread across a table. Allen said he did not take it. His account appeared in the Atlanta Journal on May 5, 1914 (AJ, 2).

Aaron Allen: Disputed words in his affidavit. Allen also said he dictated and signed a statement. He insisted that any wording saying he knew Conley had been added by someone else afterward. This was an accusation that the finished document contained something he had not agreed to swear was true (AJ, 2).

Helen Ferguson: Money to leave Atlanta. In an affidavit sworn on April 7, 1914, Ferguson said a man offered her $100, plus board and expenses, if she would leave Atlanta. According to her account, he said Frank would soon receive another trial. She said she refused the offer (AC, 7).

Helen Ferguson: Courtship and a marriage proposal. Ferguson said Jimmie Wrenn approached her under the name “J. W. Howard,” courted her, proposed marriage, and introduced Burke as his father. She alleged that they tried to persuade her to change her testimony about Mary Phagan’s pay envelope. Burke and Wrenn were later indicted over the alleged attempt. Those charges were accusations, not convictions (AC, 7, and AJ, 8).

Carrie Smith: An alleged $20 offer for a signature. Smith said a man calling himself “Maddox” offered her $20 for a signed statement about her trial testimony. He described the money as part of his payment for work on a book about the case. She said she refused. The offer alone does not prove he wanted a false statement (AJ, 9).

Marie Karst: Paid work followed by an alleged request to influence Stover. Karst said Burke paid her $2 an afternoon to approach female witnesses. She then alleged that he wanted her to live with Monteen Stover and persuade Stover to change her testimony. Karst said she refused and lost the job. Her complaint concerned that request, not simply being paid to investigate (AJ, 9).

Mary Rich: A false affidavit was submitted that she said she refused to sign. Rich disputed a defense statement saying she saw Conley leave the factory at 2:15 o’clock on the day of the murder. She said investigators presented an untrue affidavit and she refused to sign it. Her account challenged whether the document submitted in her name accurately represented what she had said (AC, 7).

Ruth Robinson: A disputed affidavit and signature. Prosecutor Hugh Dorsey accused the defense of submitting a forged affidavit in Robinson’s name. Frank’s lawyers denied the accusation and asked the judge to compare the signatures. The dispute concerned whether the document was authentic, not how a witness had been prepared for court (AJ, 9, 3).

Ivey Jones: An affidavit he called a forgery. Jones said the affidavit credited to him by the defense was forged. Frank’s lawyers disputed that accusation and urged the judge to compare signatures. His complaint therefore required examination of the actual documents and the circumstances in which they were obtained (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Frank Reese, also printed as Reeves: An alleged offer for a false confession story. Reese said Dr. George Wrenn wanted him and fellow prisoner Fred Perkerson to enter Conley’s cell, come out claiming Conley had confessed, and receive money. Wrenn denied proposing the scheme or offering a reward (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Fred Perkerson: A separate account of the proposed confession story. Perkerson also alleged that Wrenn wanted the two prisoners to pretend Conley had confessed. He said he asked why Wrenn would not do it himself. According to Perkerson, Wrenn replied that he did not want to become involved. Wrenn denied the accusation (NYT, 6, and AJ, 3).

Rev. C. B. Ragsdale: An admitted false affidavit. Ragsdale admitted that his statement claiming he overheard Conley confess was false. He alleged that he received $200 for signing it. His admission about his own false statement must be considered separately from his accusations about who arranged or paid for it (NYT, 6, and AC, 10).

R. L. Barber: An alleged payment for supporting Ragsdale’s story. Barber supplied a statement supporting the supposed confession. Ragsdale alleged that Barber received $100 for his signature. That payment allegation formed part of the disputed account of how the two statements were obtained (NYT, 6).

The Ragsdale prosecution ended in acquittals. Dan Lehon, Carlton Tedder, and Arthur Thurman were tried on charges of arranging false sworn testimony in the Ragsdale affair. On Sunday, January 31, 1915, the jury found all three not guilty. Ragsdale’s credibility had been challenged during the trial. Their prosecution must not be described as a conviction (AC, 10).

These examples vary in strength. Some involve admitted deception or an admitted false statement. Others involve disputed accusations from people who changed their stories. Each requires its own evidence.

The useful questions here are very specific: What did the witness originally say? What was offered or threatened? Did the witness understand the paper being signed? Did the finished statement match the witness’s own words? Calling everything “witness preparation” does not answer those questions.

text:
The brutal combination of $6+ diesel and high synthetic nitrogen prices is causing farmers across the Corn Belt and Northern Plains to aggressively recalculate their planting budgets.
For the upcoming crop year, the decision is coming down to risk management and cash-flow preservation, tilting acreage strongly in favor of soybeans over corn.
The Per-Acre Cash-Outlay Gap
The primary driver of acreage shifts is not necessarily which crop offers the highest theoretical gross revenue, but how much operating cash must be borrowed up front:
| Budget Factor | Corn | Soybeans | Impact on Acreage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen Needs | 160–220+ lbs/acre of synthetic N ($900+/ton anhydrous, high UAN) | Negligible (legume; fixes its own nitrogen) | Massive cost advantage for soy. |
| Diesel Burn (Field Passes) | High (deep tillage, heavy planting, sidedressing, heavy harvesting) | Moderate (light or no-till, fewer passes, lighter combine load) | Lower fuel consumption favors soy. |
| Hauling & Grain Drying | 180–240 bu/acre volume to haul; high propane/power bill to dry down | 45–65 bu/acre volume to haul; field-dries easily without gas heat | Less fuel burned at the dryer and on the road. |
| Total Non-Land Cash Outlay | ~$450 – $550+ / acre | ~$250 – $300 / acre | Soybeans require roughly half the operating credit. |
With ag operating loan interest rates remaining elevated, bankers and farm lenders are putting pressure on producers to lower their per-acre borrowing limits, making soybeans the far less risky balance-sheet proposition.
How Acreage Plans Are Shifting
1. Abandoning "Continuous Corn"
Operations that regularly run corn-on-corn (planting corn back into last year’s corn stubble) are almost entirely ditching the practice. Corn-on-corn requires:
 * Heavy fall chisel-plowing or deep ripping to chew through residue (burning massive amounts of $6 diesel).
 * An extra 30 to 50 lbs/acre of nitrogen to overcome the carbon penalty of decaying stalks.
   Growers are rotating these fields straight into soybeans to take advantage of the nitrogen credit and eliminate deep tillage passes.
2. Shifting the Traditional 50/50 Split
In core Midwest states (Illinois, Iowa, Indiana), many standard rotations run an even 50% corn and 50% soybeans. Ag economists and extension services report more growers budgeting for 60/40 or even 65/35 in favor of soybeans.
 * Shifting an extra 10% to 15% of an operation's ground into soybeans saves tens of thousands of dollars in fall pre-purchased fertilizer and fuel contracts.
 * On marginal or less productive soils where corn yields struggle to crack 150 bushels, corn is nearly impossible to pencil out at $4.20/bu against high fertilizer; those fringe acres are going straight to beans.
3. Skipping Fall Anhydrous Applications
For the corn acres that are kept, farmers are refusing to lay down fall anhydrous ammonia. Applying nitrogen in the fall at $900+ per ton locks in huge expenses months before a seed hits the ground.
 * Farmers are playing "wait-and-see," opting for spring pre-plant or in-season sidedressing instead.
 * By delaying nitrogen purchases until spring, growers retain the flexibility to swap those acres over to soybeans at the last minute if fertilizer and fuel fail to retreat over the winter.

Experience the Word of God in a new, immersive way.

It’s About Growth, Not a Checklist

As we continue through September 2026, remember that this journey is about genuine spiritual growth, not just "checking a box" for the day. Our goal is to let these scriptures transform our perspective and our priorities. If you missed a few days or are just joining us for the first time—don’t worry! Just jump right in with us today. The path to growth is always open, and there is no "behind" in this study.

Today’s Reading

In Isaiah 21–22, the prophet receives heavy visions concerning the nations, beginning with the fall of Babylon and distress over Edom and Arabia. Chapter 22 shifts to the "Valley of Vision," delivering a piercing indictment against Jerusalem for relying on military defenses and carnal celebration rather than turning in humble repentance to the Maker who fashioned it all. Turning to the New Testament, John 14 offers profound comfort to troubled hearts as Jesus prepares His disciples for His departure, declaring, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me." Jesus promises the gift of the Holy Spirit as the Helper, reassuring believers that they will not be left as orphans and bestowing His supernatural peace that surpasses worldly understanding. This video is designed to help you focus on the text without distraction, featuring modern visuals and a clear, read-along experience.

Join the Global Community

This project is an outreach of the Richmond Church of Christ in Kentucky, connecting brothers and sisters from across the globe—including our communities in Nigeria, India, and South Africa. NEWS: Massive lines are forming outside Miami Immigration Court after the court shifted most non-detained cases from virtual hearings back to mandatory in-person appearances beginning Sept. 8.

The court at 333 S. Miami Avenue has seen crowds wrapping around the building, with immigration attorneys reporting waits of up to two hours as people try to get inside before their scheduled hearings. 

The stakes are high: missing an immigration hearing can result in an in absentia removal order, meaning a judge can order someone deported when they fail to appear. Attorneys have warned that long security lines themselves could create problems for people who arrive at the courthouse on time but cannot reach the courtroom before their cases are called. 

DOJ rules still permit immigration judges to conduct some proceedings by video or telephone, and judges retain authority in certain circumstances to waive appearances. But Miami’s default for affected non-detained cases is now in-person attendance. 

The scenes offer a visible reminder of just how large the immigration-court workload has become: move thousands of cases off Zoom and back into one courthouse, and the backlog suddenly becomes a line you can see. https://t.co/gJQbMDLYfn
