text:
In the quiet of this evening hour, as shadows lengthen across the earth, we gather our scattered thoughts and turn to the Apostle Paul’s tender exhortation in his second letter to the Corinthians: “Rejoice… be perfected.” These words were penned not in the flush of triumph but from the crucible of pastoral sorrow. The church at Corinth, still reeling from divisions, immorality, and challenges to apostolic authority, needed both rebuke and embrace. Paul, having written with severity in his first epistle, now closes his second with a father’s final plea for unity, joy, and completion in Christ.

The historical setting is vivid. Corinth, a bustling crossroads of commerce and philosophy, mirrored the tensions of the early Church. Factions claimed allegiance to Paul, Apollos, or Cephas; some denied the resurrection; others tolerated grave sin. Into this fractured community the Apostle sends his closing charge. St. John Chrysostom, preaching in the golden-tongued eloquence of Antioch and Constantinople, explains that true rejoicing flows only from restored harmony: “Rejoice not in abundance of goods, but in the mending of souls.” Perfection, he insists, is not an abstract ideal but the practical knitting together of minds and hearts so that the God of love and peace may dwell among them.

The Catena Aurea preserves for us the wisdom of earlier Fathers who read these verses as a summary of the entire Christian life. St. Augustine teaches that to “be perfected” is to be restored to the image of the Trinity through charity that casts out division. Where peace reigns, he writes, the Holy Spirit makes His temple. In the age of persecutions, when bishops like Ignatius of Antioch were led to Rome in chains, this same call sustained the faithful: rejoice in the Lord always, and let nothing remain broken in the body of Christ. The martyrs did not seek earthly consolation; their joy was the seal of their perfection.

Beloved, this evening we too stand at the close of another day marked by noise and fragmentation. The same God who promised His presence to a reconciled Corinth offers it to us. Let us examine whether any breach remains in our charity, any faction in our hearts. May we heed the Apostle’s final benediction, living in peace so that the God of peace may truly be with us.

text:
No. It was already tried and shutdown. The two state solution was already tried by Israel and it was rejected by the Palestinians. And it’s the Palestinian government that rejected it. Not all the Palestinian people. Per Grok:

“Jewish and later Israeli leadership accepted or proposed versions of a two-state or partition arrangement on several major occasions, while Palestinian leadership rejected the specific terms offered at key turning points. https://t.co/WWsR6bMATd 
The 1947 UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181) called for separate Jewish and Arab states plus an international zone for Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted it. Arab states and Palestinian leadership rejected it, and war followed. Earlier, the 1937 Peel Commission partition proposal was accepted in principle by Jewish leaders and rejected by Arab leaders. https://t.co/iAHkZ71gtK 
After 1967, the Oslo Accords (1993) marked Israel’s formal recognition of the PLO and creation of the Palestinian Authority as a step toward self-rule, with the stated goal of a negotiated two-state outcome. In 2000 at Camp David, Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered a Palestinian state on most of the West Bank and all of Gaza plus arrangements for parts of East Jerusalem. Yasser Arafat did not accept the package and did not present a detailed counter-offer; the talks collapsed and the Second Intifada began. Israel later accepted the Clinton Parameters; the Palestinian side did not. @world-politics 
In 2008 Prime Minister Ehud Olmert presented Mahmoud Abbas with a map that would have given a Palestinian state roughly 93–95 percent of the West Bank (with equivalent land swaps from Israel), a link between the West Bank and Gaza, shared or internationally administered arrangements for the Old City/holy sites, and a limited humanitarian intake of refugees. Abbas did not sign. Israel also unilaterally withdrew from Gaza in 2005. https://t.co/IOHWK9iYNL 
Palestinian negotiators have cited remaining gaps on exact borders, the scale of settlement blocs Israel would keep, sovereignty over the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif, and the “right of return” for 1948 refugees and descendants as reasons the offers were insufficient. Israeli governments after 2009, especially under Netanyahu, have been far more reluctant to revive the same framework. The pattern of earlier Israeli-accepted partitions and detailed offers is a matter of public diplomatic record.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​“

Wed, Sep 16

Will You Pray With Us?

Dear Friends,

Will you please pray with us for those who call our Hotline? Each week we answer dozens of calls from those struggling with an unexpected pregnancy, many who share that they feel alone, scared, and unsure where to turn.

“Is this a Hotline? I just need someone to help me with my emotions. I am four weeks pregnant and was kind of excited until I told the father and now he's been pressuring me to "terminate it." I definitely don't want to do that but I'm so let down and shocked by his reaction.

— Nashville, TN

“I'm pregnant but unsure what to do or how to tell my boyfriend. Please help me, I'm so lost!

— Oregon

“I just found out I'm two months pregnant. I'm living with my older sister and she thinks I should have an abortion. I know I don't want to kill it and go through that. But can you help me find some resources for support? I don't know where to start with what I will need.

— Fort Wayne, IN

Often, we can hear the anxiety and distress in callers' voices. We ask if we can pray with them, and many express their appreciation for this.

We believe in the power of prayer, and know God can intervene in these difficult situations. Let's ask God to guide, protect, and be with each caller!

We're so grateful these callers found their way to ProLife Across America, so we can provide them with a listening ear and with a connection to pro-life pregnancy support in their local area.
